hook.text: Take a table that gains eight thousand rows a day. Rebuild all of it every night, and two years in, each run reprocesses over six million rows to add eight thousand.

hook-snail.text: An incremental model processes only the new ones.

plan.text: Seven questions on how it does that and where it goes wrong: which rows count as new, what makes a rerun safe, and why the full rebuild never quite goes away.

when.text: Question one. When do you use an incremental model, and what's the catch? When a table is large and mostly appends, like events, logs or page views, so a full rebuild is too slow or too expensive.

when-flat.text: An incremental run processes one day's arrivals, so its cost stays flat while the rebuild's climbs. By day seven hundred thirty, the rebuild does seven hundred fifty-five times the work.

when-catch.text: The catch is what that shortcut assumes: a reliable way to find the new rows, correct handling of rows that arrive late or change, and a tested way to recover when the table drifts.

when-spikes.text: Recovery means a full rebuild, and its cost grows too. Each spike here is a scheduled full refresh, every sixty days.

when-not.text: So when do you choose incremental over a full table rebuild? Only when the table is big and append-mostly. If it's small, or changes broadly every run, a plain table is simpler and safer.

filter.text: Question two. How does an incremental model actually filter new rows? With a watermark: the latest timestamp already loaded. On an incremental run, a guard adds one condition to the model: only source rows newer than the maximum in the model's own table.

filter-run.text: On the page's tables, the model holds events through January fourteenth, and the source has twenty-four. The filter loads the ten after the watermark.

filter-arrive.text: Then three more land. Event twenty-five has the same timestamp as the new watermark. Twenty-six happened on the twenty-second and arrived late. Twenty-seven is simply new.

filter-strict.text: A strict greater-than finds only twenty-seven. The other two are never loaded, and nothing errors.

filter-gte.text: Greater-than-or-equal, plus deduplication, catches the tie: twenty-five comes in, and twenty-four, read again, is skipped. But twenty-six is older than the watermark, so it's still missed.

filter-overlap.text: So production models re-read an overlap window, here the last three days, and merge on a stable key. The window reads seven rows, and all three new ones land.

filter-width.text: Make the window as wide as your data arrives late. A wider one re-reads more on every run, and an event later than the window still slips past.

filter-seq.text: The other way out is a change sequence the source guarantees only ever grows, so nothing can land behind the watermark.

this.text: Question three. What is the "this" variable in dbt? It's the model's own table in the warehouse, the one the filter takes its maximum from.

this-first.text: On the very first run that table doesn't exist yet, so the incremental check returns false, the guard is skipped, and the model loads everything.

key.text: Question four. What is the unique key config on an incremental model, and what does it control? It tells a strategy that updates or replaces rows how to match an incoming row to the one already in the table.

key-append.text: Without it, rows are appended. The overlap window read seven events, four of them already loaded, so the table now holds thirty-one rows for twenty-seven events. Retry the run, and it's thirty-eight.

key-merge.text: Set the unique key to the event ID, and a merge updates the four it already has and inserts the three it doesn't: twenty-seven rows, and twenty-seven again on a retry. Delete, then insert, on the same key, gets there too.

key-dup.text: But the key isn't checked. Had the source sent event twenty-seven twice, the same merge would insert both copies, without an error.

key-dup-fail.text: On the next run, Postgres refuses the merge outright: one row can't be updated twice.

key-test.text: So put a uniqueness test on the key.

idem.text: Question five. What is an idempotent rebuild, and why does it matter? Idempotent means running the build again produces the same result. It matters because pipelines retry: a job that crashes after writing will run again.

idem-blind.text: Load the page's customer dimension with a blind insert, and a retry doubles it: twelve customers become twenty-four rows.

idem-rebuild.text: Rebuild it from the source instead. Postgres has no create or replace table, so the page drops and recreates it inside one transaction. Run it twice, and the twelve rows are identical.

idem-fail.text: And if a rebuild fails after the drop, the transaction rolls back, and the old table is still there, all twelve rows.

idem-two.text: Those are the two routes. Rebuild from the source while the table is small enough, and once it isn't, merge on a key.

merge.text: Question six. How does a merge support idempotent upserts? It matches each staged row to the target on a key. A match updates, and no match inserts.

merge-run.text: Here Ben has a new name, and Dee is new. The first merge updates Ben and inserts Dee: four customers.

merge-rerun.text: Run the same batch again, and it matches both, writes the values they already hold, and inserts nothing: still four. A blind insert of that batch into the original three, twice, leaves seven rows.

merge-dbt.text: It's the statement a merge-style incremental strategy runs, keyed on the unique key, though which strategy you get depends on the adapter and on your config.

merge-delete.text: What a merge can't do is delete. A row removed from the source never reaches the batch, so the target keeps it.

refresh.text: Question seven. What is the difference between dbt run with the full refresh flag, and a normal incremental run? A normal run filters to new rows and merges them in. A full refresh ignores the incremental check, and rebuilds the table from every source row.

refresh-why.text: So why are periodic full refreshes still needed? Because incremental logic only sees what passes its filter.

refresh-drift.text: Take the strict filter's table from question two, and delete event three upstream. The next normal run finds nothing, and the table is wrong in three rows: two events missing, and one that no longer exists.

refresh-fix.text: A full refresh reads all twenty-six and matches the source exactly. It's also how a schema change gets applied.

refresh-cost.text: But it's the expensive run. On the chart's table, the last refresh reprocesses almost six million rows, and over two years, the twelve refreshes are eighty-seven percent of everything the incremental model processed.

refresh-rule.text: So treat incremental as an optimization over a correct full rebuild. And don't let a refresh schedule stand in for a correct filter: for the largest models, a full refresh may not be practical at all.

next.text: Every fix here came down to a query: a filter, a deduplication, a merge on a key. Next: advanced SQL, the queries inside the models.
next.spoken: Every fix here came down to a query: a filter, a deduplication, a merge on a key. Next: advanced sequel, the queries inside the models.

filter-micro.text: Since dbt one point nine, the microbatch strategy takes the filter out of your hands: set an event time and a batch size, and dbt builds one idempotent batch per day, re-processes lookback batches for late rows, and backfills any date range.
